Context/Background:
Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second leading cause of male cancer-related deaths. To date, the strategy to develop therapies for PCa mainly focuses on blocking either the activity or the transcriptional targets of known oncogenes. While the PCa transcriptome has been studied for decades, we have little knowledge of the translatome. The importance of this post-transcriptional regulation is underscored by the realization that RNA transcript levels are a poor proxy for protein abundance.

Translation initiation is a tightly regulated step critical to maintain the accurate protein dosage of growth and survival factors in cells.Importantly, emerging studies show that translation factors act in a rapid, selective, and robust manner to control the production of specific proteins. One of the most important of those factors is the RNA-binding protein and translation factor eukaryotic initiation factor 4A (eIF4A), which helps to unwind structured 5′ UTRs to increase translation initiation of select mRNAs in cancer.

Pharmacologic inhibition of eIF4A with zotatifin, a clinical compound, suppressed tumor growth in vivo, reducing both primary tumor growth and metastasis.

To understand how the inhibitor works mechanistically, we investigated the effect of zotatifin on the PCa translatome and proteome after a short treatment, as translation is one of the most rapid steps of gene expression. We performed ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) and MS after 6 h of zotatifin treatment in 22Rv1 cell xenografts in vivo. While MS analysis assesses the effect of zotatifin on the global protein landscape in tumors, Ribo-seq can capture translation efficiency genome-wide at single-nucleotide resolution. Ribo-seq analysis revealed 554 downregulated transcripts at the translational level (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.01 and log2FC ≤ −0.3). On the other hand, MS analysis showed that 339 proteins were downregulated upon zotatifin treatment (p value < 0.05 and log2FC ≤ −0.2). Next, we analyzed genes that are downregulated at the translational level as well as at the protein level by cross-referencing the two datasets using less stringent cutoffs (Ribo-seq FDR < 0.05 and log2FC < 0 and MS p value < 0.05 and log2(FC) < 0).
Prompt: From the genes that are downregulated at both translational level and protein level, prioritize a few targets that are particularly relevant to prostate cancer.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
Zotatifin is a clinical eIF4A inhibitor tested in 22Rv1 prostate cancer (PCa) cell xenografts in vivo. After 6 h treatment, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) identified 554 downregulated transcripts (FDR<0.01, log2FC≤−0.3), and mass spectrometry (MS) found 339 downregulated proteins (p<0.05, log2FC≤−0.2). Cross‐referencing with relaxed cutoffs (Ribo FDR<0.05 & log2FC<0; MS p<0.05 & log2FC<0) yielded 108 genes downregulated at both translational and protein levels. Here, we prioritize among those common hits to highlight targets of particular relevance to prostate cancer.

• eIF4A  
• translation initiation  
• prostate cancer  
• translatome  

Candidate Genes  
AR, CDK4, HIF1A, FOLH1

Despite some upregulation of muscle-related and keratinization programs, core cancer‐related modules—mRNA processing/splicing and cell-cycle regulators—are strongly downregulated (particularly in GO, Reactome, and Hallmark). The modest KEGG_2016 uptrend likely reflects tumor stroma remodeling rather than cancer cell proliferation.

Key Genes/Proteins (leading edge, downregulated)  
| Gene   | Direction | Role/Function                                         | Pathway(s)                                                                                                           |
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| AR     | Down      | Androgen receptor, steroid‐hormone TF driving PCa      | Prostate cancer (ORA), “Pathways in cancer,” cell‐cycle modules (G2-M/E2F)                                            |
| CDK4   | Down      | Cyclin‐dependent kinase regulating G1/S progression   | Hallmark G2-M Checkpoint, E2F Targets, “Pathways in cancer”                                                          |
| HIF1A  | Down      | Hypoxia‐inducible TF, master metabolic regulator      | Central carbon metabolism in cancer, mTORC1 Signaling, Proteoglycans in cancer                                        |
| FOLH1  | Down      | Folate hydrolase (PSMA), prostate‐specific marker      | Not captured in cancer‐focused ORA (emerges from protein data as PSMA, a clinically exploited imaging/theranostic target) |

Comparisons & Confidence  
AR, CDK4, and HIF1A are down in both assays and appear in multiple cancer‐relevant pathways—highest confidence. FOLH1 (PSMA) is robustly down at the protein level but shows weaker PubMed/network centrality; despite low composite score, its prostate specificity (PSMA) makes it a compelling secondary target.  

Implications  
• AR downregulation suggests zo­tatifin may blunt AR‐driven transcription/alternative splicing programs in PCa.  
• CDK4 loss aligns with G2-M/E2F checkpoint disruption, supporting combination with CDK4/6 inhibitors.  
• HIF1A reduction implicates impaired hypoxia and metabolic adaptation—potentially sensitizing tumors to anti-angiogenic or metabolic agents.  
• PSMA (FOLH1) downregulation warrants evaluation of imaging/theranostic modalities under translation inhibition.  

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate PSMA (FOLH1) downregulation by IHC or PET imaging in 22Rv1 xenografts.  
2. Test synergy of zotatifin with CDK4/6 inhibitors in vitro.  
3. Assess AR splice variant levels (e.g., AR-V7) post-zotatifin to clarify AR axis modulation.  
4. Confirm key themes: strong downregulation of cell‐cycle/replication (observed), mRNA splicing (observed), and central carbon metabolism (observed).

• PMC6255907 – Hypoxia–androgen interplay controls metabolic resistance mechanisms in PCa.
